column3: What are the four main structural alternatives to open-ended Medicaid matching?
column4:
• Block grant — fixed federal amount per state, growing by a set trend
  • Per capita cap — fixed federal amount per enrollee, times actual enrollment
  • Reduced or uniform match rate — keep the structure, lower the FMAP (e.g. cut the 90 percent expansion rate)
  • Capped allotment for a subgroup — cap only certain populations or services


The organising question for all four: who bears the risk of costs exceeding projections — the federal government (status quo), or the states. Everything else is detail about how quickly and in what circumstances the risk transfers.

column3: How does a per capita cap differ from a block grant, and why does the difference matter?
column4:
A block grant fixes the total federal dollars regardless of how many people enroll. A per capita cap fixes federal dollars per enrollee, so the total flexes with enrollment.

A per capita cap therefore preserves countercyclicality (more enrollees in a recession still means more federal money) while a block grant does not. What a per capita cap does not preserve is protection against cost growth per person — epidemics, a new expensive therapy, or an aging caseload all fall on the state.

column3: What are the key design parameters of a per capita cap?
column4:
• Base year — which year's spending sets the starting amount (locks in existing state variation, rewarding high spenders)
  • Growth trend — CPI-M, CPI-U plus a factor, GDP plus a factor, or a fixed percentage
  • Eligibility group granularity — one cap or separate caps for children, adults, aged, disabled
  • Rebasing — whether and how often the base resets
  • Exclusions — DSH, administration, territories, IHS, public health emergencies


The growth trend does nearly all the fiscal work. A trend even one point below actual per capita cost growth compounds into very large state shortfalls over ten years, which is why CBO scores of capped proposals grow steeply in the out-years.

column3: Why does eligibility-group granularity matter in a per capita cap?
column4:
Because per-enrollee costs differ by an order of magnitude across groups. A single blended cap would penalize states whose caseload shifts toward the aged and disabled and reward states whose caseload shifts toward children — changes largely outside state control.

Group-specific caps fix that but introduce classification incentives: the state gains by recording enrollees in whichever category carries the more generous cap, so the design has to police category assignment.

column3: Trace the history of Medicaid block grant and cap proposals.
column4:
• 1981 — Reagan proposed a capped federal contribution; Congress instead enacted a temporary FMAP reduction
  • 1995 — the "MediGrant" block grant passed Congress and was vetoed by President Clinton
  • 2003 — Bush administration proposed optional block-grant-style allotments
  • 2017 — AHCA, BCRA, and Graham-Cassidy all included per capita caps with a block grant option
  • 2020 — CMS's Healthy Adult Opportunity invited states to take capped funding for expansion adults via 1115


The pattern is consistent: capped financing is proposed roughly once a decade, generally fails, and each attempt refines the technical design. Healthy Adult Opportunity is notable for attempting by waiver what Congress had declined to legislate; no state adopted it and it was rescinded.

column3: State the honest case for capped federal Medicaid financing.
column4:
• Federal budget predictability, and a hard constraint on a fast-growing mandatory program
  • Removes the state incentive created by matching, where a state buys a dollar of services for 20-50 cents and therefore over-spends relative to what it would choose with its own money
  • Weakens the payoff to financing gimmicks (provider taxes, IGT recycling) that exist mainly to maximize the draw
  • Paired with regulatory relief, could let states redesign benefits and delivery without waiver negotiation


The match-rate distortion argument is the strongest one and is standard public finance: an open-ended matching grant is a price subsidy on state spending. Learn to state it before critiquing it.

column3: State the case against capped federal Medicaid financing.
column4:
• Transfers cost risk to states that cannot run deficits, so shortfalls become eligibility, benefit, or provider payment cuts
  • Destroys or weakens countercyclicality, cutting exactly when need rises
  • Locks in historical state spending variation as a permanent baseline
  • Cannot absorb epidemics, disasters, or new high-cost therapies without ad hoc congressional action
  • Aggregate savings are largely a cost shift, not efficiency: the coverage losses in CBO scores are the mechanism by which savings are achieved


The strongest version is not "states would cut" but "states would be forced to cut, at the worst possible time, and the design offers no mechanism other than cuts." Any serious cap proposal needs an explicit recession valve.

column3: What is a maintenance of effort (MOE) requirement?
column4:
A condition requiring states to keep eligibility standards, methods, or spending at least at a specified prior level as a condition of receiving federal funds.

Examples: the ACA's eligibility MOE for children through 2019, and FFCRA's continuous enrollment condition attached to the 6.2 point FMAP bump. MOEs are how the federal government prevents states from pocketing an inducement while cutting elsewhere — and they are the reason states resist temporary FMAP bumps that carry strings.

column3: What is an automatic countercyclical FMAP, and why do analysts favour it?
column4:
A standing formula that raises the federal match automatically when a state's economic conditions deteriorate — typically triggered by the state unemployment rate or its change — rather than requiring new legislation in each recession.

Both ARRA (2009) and FFCRA (2020) were enacted with lags after the downturn began. GAO, MACPAC, and a broad range of economists have recommended an automatic trigger; the objections are the difficulty of choosing a trigger that turns off cleanly and congressional reluctance to give up discretion.

column3: What was the Arkansas "private option"?
column4:
An 1115 demonstration (2014) that used Medicaid funds to buy qualified health plan coverage on the ACA marketplace for expansion adults, rather than enrolling them in Medicaid managed care.

The political function was to let a conservative state expand coverage while describing the result as private insurance. The trade: marketplace plans pay commercial-level rates, so provider access improves but per-enrollee cost is higher. Later renamed Arkansas Works, and the model was adopted in modified form by New Hampshire.

column3: What federal tests must a premium assistance arrangement satisfy?
column4:
Cost effectiveness (the premium plus wraparound must not exceed what direct Medicaid coverage would cost) and wraparound coverage (the state must cover any Medicaid benefits the private plan omits, and cost sharing above Medicaid limits).

The wraparound obligation is what makes premium assistance administratively difficult: the enrollee holds a commercial card, but the state remains liable for the gap. Several 1115s have waived or narrowed the wraparound for expansion adults, which is where the real policy fight has been.

column3: What was distinctive about Indiana's Healthy Indiana Plan (HIP 2.0)?
column4:
It used POWER accounts — health-savings-account-style accounts funded by monthly enrollee contributions of about 2 percent of income. Paying in bought the richer HIP Plus benefit (including vision and dental); not paying dropped enrollees above the poverty line out of coverage entirely, and those below it into a leaner HIP Basic with copays.

The theory was "consumer skin in the game." The evaluation evidence is that contributions functioned largely as an enrollment barrier: a substantial share of eligible people never made a first payment, with the effect concentrated among the poorest. Compare with the RAND HIE finding that cost sharing reduces effective and ineffective care alike.

column3: Name several distinct state approaches to expansion beyond straight adoption.
column4:
• Arkansas — premium assistance into marketplace plans
  • Indiana — POWER accounts and contributions
  • Michigan — Healthy Michigan, with health risk assessments and healthy behavior incentives
  • Montana — expansion paired with a voluntary workforce training program
  • Utah — partial expansion (to 100% FPL) sought first, later full expansion after CMS refused enhanced match for partial
  • Georgia — Pathways: coverage to 100% FPL conditioned on work, without expansion


A useful lesson: CMS's refusal to grant the 90 percent enhanced match for partial expansion (below 138 percent FPL) was decisive in pushing several states to full expansion. Match rate policy shaped state design more than any waiver term did.

column3: What is Georgia Pathways to Coverage, and what has it demonstrated?
column4:
A non-expansion 1115 program launched July 2023 covering adults to 100 percent FPL conditioned on 80 hours a month of qualifying activity. Enrollment has stayed a tiny fraction of the eligible population — roughly 16,000 by early 2026 against an eligible pool in the hundreds of thousands.

GAO reported in 2025 that the majority of program spending went to administration rather than health care. Georgia has since eased reporting from monthly to at application and annual renewal, and CMS extended the demonstration through the end of 2026. As the only operating work-conditioned program, it is the closest thing to a live test of the 2027 federal requirement.

column3: What are the main design parameters of a Medicaid work requirement?
column4:
• Hours threshold and what activities count
  • Reporting frequency — monthly versus at application and renewal
  • Verification method — enrollee self-report versus state data matching (ex parte)
  • Exemption scope and whether exemptions are automatic or must be claimed
  • Consequence — termination, lockout period, or suspension
  • Notice, outreach, and reinstatement pathways


The evidence points at reporting and verification, not the hours threshold, as the binding parameter. Most affected enrollees already meet the hours; coverage loss comes from failing to document compliance. A design that verifies through payroll and other state data rather than enrollee submission changes the outcome far more than adjusting the hours would.

column3: What is the "ordeal" framing of administrative burden, and how does it apply here?
column4:
From Nichols and Zeckhauser (1982): a costly, non-monetary hurdle can improve targeting if the cost is higher for the less needy, screening them out. Applied to Medicaid, reporting requirements are defended as sorting the deserving from the undeserving.

The empirical objection is that the ordeal is not more costly for the less needy. People with unstable work, disabilities, low literacy, or no reliable internet face the highest compliance costs — so the burden sorts on capacity to navigate bureaucracy rather than on need or on work effort. See the Arkansas evidence in deck 3.

column3: What are the competing theories of what a work requirement is for?
column4:
• Behavioral — coverage creates work disincentives; conditioning it raises employment
  • Reciprocity / desert — able-bodied adults should contribute in exchange for public benefits, independent of employment effects
  • Fiscal — the requirement reduces enrollment and therefore spending; savings are the point


Worth separating because they imply different success criteria and different evidence. Arkansas's data speak directly to the first (no employment effect) and the third (large coverage loss). They cannot resolve the second, which is a normative claim. Debates go in circles when participants argue different theories past each other.

column3: What does the evidence suggest about premiums and cost sharing in Medicaid?
column4:
Premiums reduce enrollment substantially, with the largest effects at the lowest incomes. Cost sharing reduces utilization of both high-value and low-value care, and generates little net saving once foregone care and collection costs are counted — providers frequently cannot collect nominal copays from very low income patients.

Grounded in the RAND Health Insurance Experiment (cost sharing reduces appropriate and inappropriate care alike, with the poorest and sickest suffering health effects), the Oregon experiment, and evaluations of Indiana, Iowa, and Michigan. The design implication: cost sharing in Medicaid works mainly as an enrollment lever, not a utilization-steering lever.

column3: What are "healthy behavior incentives," and how have they performed?
column4:
Programs conditioning reduced contributions or richer benefits on completing a health risk assessment, a wellness visit, or health goals — used in Michigan, Iowa, Indiana, and elsewhere.

Evaluations consistently find low awareness and low completion rates, with participation skewed toward enrollees already engaged with care. They add administrative complexity for modest measurable effect. As a design lesson: incentives that require the enrollee to understand a multi-step contingency perform poorly in this population.

column3: What is the theoretical case for Medicaid managed care, and what is the corresponding risk?
column4:
Case: capitation makes a single entity residual claimant on total cost, creating incentives to substitute cheap prevention and care management for expensive acute care, and giving the state budget predictability.
Risk: the same incentive rewards underprovision and favourable selection, and enrollees have limited ability to detect or respond to either.

Everything in managed care regulation — actuarial soundness, MLR, network adequacy, EQR, risk adjustment, appeals — is an attempt to keep the first effect while suppressing the second. Judge any managed care reform by which of the two it strengthens.

column3: Why is risk adjustment central to Medicaid managed care design?
column4:
Without it, plans profit more by attracting healthy enrollees than by managing care well. Risk adjustment pays more for predictably expensive enrollees so that selection is less profitable than efficiency.

Medicaid risk adjustment is harder than Medicare's: diagnosis data are less complete, enrollment spells are shorter, and a large share of variation is social rather than clinical. Imperfect risk adjustment leaves residual selection incentives — the mechanism behind the infant health disparities found under Texas managed care (Kuziemko et al., deck 3).

column3: What levers does a state have in managed care procurement?
column4:
• Number of plans awarded (competition versus scale and administrative simplicity)
  • Scoring weights on quality, network, and prior performance
  • Mandatory regions and statewide versus regional awards
  • Auto-assignment rules that reward quality
  • Contract terms: withholds, incentive pools, MLR remittance, directed payments


Procurement is the single most consequential and least studied Medicaid policy instrument: an RFP rewrites the incentives of most of a state's program at once, and awards are frequently litigated by losing bidders.

column3: What are risk corridors, withholds, and incentive pools?
column4:
• Risk corridor — the state and plan share gains and losses outside a band around expected costs, limiting plan risk
  • Withhold — the state holds back a share of capitation, returned if the plan hits quality targets
  • Incentive pool — additional dollars distributed for performance


Risk corridors are the standard tool when a state moves a new population into managed care and neither party can price it — as in early MLTSS or during COVID. They deliberately blunt the capitation incentive in exchange for protecting both sides from mispricing.

column3: What are Oregon's Coordinated Care Organizations (CCOs)?
column4:
Regional entities holding a global budget for physical, behavioral, and (increasingly) oral health for Medicaid enrollees in their area, governed locally, and contractually bound to hold per capita cost growth to a fixed rate — originally 3.4 percent a year — with quality incentive payments attached.

Launched 2012 under an 1115 with federal investment in exchange for the growth commitment. The design features worth extracting: a hard growth target, local governance including community members, flexible "health-related services" spending, and integration of behavioral and physical health under one budget.

column3: Name several state Medicaid accountable-care models and what distinguishes each.
column4:
• Oregon CCOs — regional global budgets with a fixed growth cap
  • Colorado RAEs — regional accountable entities combining physical and behavioral health administration
  • Minnesota IHPs — provider-led total cost of care contracts with shared savings
  • Massachusetts ACOs — accountable care organizations within managed care, with behavioral health and LTSS community partners
  • North Carolina — managed care launch paired with Healthy Opportunities Pilots for social needs


Note the recurring variable: whether accountability sits with a plan, a provider organization, or a regional entity. That choice determines who can actually be held to a total cost of care number, and who has the balance sheet to bear risk.

column3: What were DSRIP waivers?
column4:
Delivery System Reform Incentive Payment programs — 1115 demonstrations (New York, Texas, California, and others, roughly 2010-2020) that made large federal payments to providers contingent on completing delivery system transformation projects and hitting performance milestones.

Their political function was often to convert expiring supplemental payment pools into something reform-shaped. Evaluations were mixed to disappointing: process milestones were widely met, but effects on cost and outcomes were hard to detect, and much of the money followed pre-existing payment flows. Most were not renewed. The cautionary lesson is that paying for "transformation" activity is not the same as paying for results.

column3: What are health-related social needs (HRSN) initiatives in Medicaid?
column4:
Coverage of non-clinical services — housing supports, medically tailored meals and produce, case management for social needs — for targeted high-need enrollees, financed through 1115 demonstrations or through managed care "in lieu of services."

CMS issued a framework in 2023 setting expectations: targeted populations, defined service menus, evaluation, and a cap on the share of spending. Note the standing limits — Medicaid generally cannot pay rent, only housing transition and tenancy sustaining services. California's CalAIM Community Supports and North Carolina's Healthy Opportunities Pilots are the flagship examples.

column3: What is CalAIM?
column4:
California Advancing and Innovating Medi-Cal — a broad 1115/1915(b) restructuring featuring Enhanced Care Management (intensive care coordination for defined high-need populations) and Community Supports (a menu of optional substitute services plans may offer, from housing navigation to medically tailored meals to recuperative care).

It is the largest single test of the HRSN approach, and also folded in justice-involved reentry services, population health management, and a statewide managed care procurement. Its scale makes it the case study most likely to generate usable evidence about whether social-needs services pay for themselves.

column3: What is a hospital global budget, and where has Medicaid participated in one?
column4:
A fixed annual revenue amount for a hospital regardless of volume, which converts admissions from a revenue source into a cost. Maryland's all-payer model (including Medicaid) is the leading U.S. example; Pennsylvania's Rural Health Model applies the idea to rural hospitals; Vermont's all-payer ACO model is a related design.

Global budgets are the strongest available tool against volume incentives and are particularly suited to rural hospitals with unavoidably low volume. The difficulty is setting and updating the budget without either windfalls or forced closures, and preventing service reductions in place of efficiency.

column3: What was the ACA primary care "fee bump," and what did it show?
column4:
A requirement (2013-2014, fully federally funded) that Medicaid pay Medicare rates for specified primary care services. Appointment availability for new Medicaid patients rose measurably during the bump and fell back after it expired in states that did not continue it.

The natural experiment is unusually clean: a large, temporary, exogenous price change. It establishes that Medicaid access responds to payment rates — an unsurprising result that nonetheless matters, because it means access problems are partly a purchased outcome rather than an inherent feature of the program.

column3: Why is raising Medicaid payment rates harder than it looks?
column4:
• Cost is immediate and large; the access gain is diffuse and slow
  • States pay a share of every dollar, so a rate increase competes directly with eligibility and benefits in the same budget
  • Rate increases are hard to reverse politically once providers build them into operations
  • In managed care, the state cannot simply set a rate — it must use directed payments or minimum fee schedules


This is why supplemental and directed payments, financed by provider taxes, became the dominant route: they raise provider revenue while limiting the call on state general funds. The 2025 law's simultaneous restriction of both is a significant tightening of that route.

column3: What tools do states use to manage Medicaid drug spending given the open formulary requirement?
column4:
• Preferred drug lists with prior authorization for non-preferred drugs
  • Supplemental rebates negotiated on top of federal rebates in exchange for preferred placement
  • Single statewide PDL across fee-for-service and managed care, to maximize negotiating leverage
  • Pharmacy carve-out to fee-for-service, capturing rebates directly
  • Step therapy, quantity limits, and clinical criteria


The binding constraint is that a state cannot simply exclude a covered manufacturer's drug, so all management is friction rather than exclusion. That makes prior authorization the central instrument and its administrative burden the central complaint.

column3: What is the "subscription" or Netflix model for Medicaid drug purchasing?
column4:
A state pays a manufacturer a fixed annual amount for unlimited access to a drug for its Medicaid (and often correctional) population, converting a per-unit price into a flat fee and eliminating the budget penalty for treating more people.

Louisiana and Washington both used it for hepatitis C antivirals, where the clinical case for treating everyone was strong and per-unit prices made that fiscally impossible. It is the cleanest example of a payment model redesigned around a specific clinical and budgetary geometry — and it does not generalize to drugs without those properties.

column3: What is the Cell and Gene Therapy Access Model?
column4:
A CMS model in which the federal government negotiates outcomes-based agreements with manufacturers of sickle cell gene therapies on behalf of participating state Medicaid programs, so states get consistent pricing and payment tied to results.

It addresses a structural problem: one-time therapies with seven-figure prices concentrate cost in a single year for a payer whose enrollees churn, so the payer bearing the cost may not capture the savings. Federal negotiation solves states' scale disadvantage; it does not solve the churn-driven mismatch between who pays and who benefits.

column3: What are the main design tools for reducing churn?
column4:
• Continuous eligibility — 12 months, or multi-year for young children
  • Ex parte renewal using existing data sources
  • Reasonable compatibility thresholds that avoid demanding documentation for small discrepancies
  • Longer reasonable-opportunity and reconsideration periods after a procedural termination
  • Integrated eligibility across Medicaid, SNAP, and TANF so one data update serves all


All of these trade a small amount of "ineligible person-months" for a large reduction in "eligible person losing coverage." Which side of that trade a policy lands on is essentially a values choice about which error type matters more — the same structure as a type I / type II error trade-off.

column3: What is the case for multi-year continuous eligibility for young children?
column4:
Nearly all children under 6 in low-income families remain eligible year to year, so redetermination mostly generates paperwork and gaps rather than accurate exits. Continuity in early childhood is when the long-run returns to coverage (documented in the childhood Medicaid literature) are largest.

Oregon's 1115 provides continuous eligibility from birth to age 6, with other states following in modified form. The counterargument is fiscal — the state pays for months in which some children would have been ineligible — and the empirical question is how large that share actually is.

column3: What is the Basic Health Program?
column4:
An ACA option (section 1331) letting a state cover people between 138 and 200 percent FPL in a state-contracted plan financed by 95 percent of the federal subsidies those people would have received on the marketplace.

Minnesota (MinnesotaCare), New York (Essential Plan), and Oregon have used it. Its design purpose is churn: it puts the population just above the Medicaid line into a program with Medicaid-like cost sharing, so income fluctuations across 138 percent FPL do not force a change of plan and provider.

column3: What is a Medicaid "buy-in" or state public option?
column4:
Letting people above Medicaid income limits purchase coverage that uses Medicaid's provider network, payment rates, or administrative machinery — either as a marketplace product or as a direct state program.

The attraction is Medicaid's low payment rates; that is also the obstacle, since providers resist expanding Medicaid-rate volume. Most enacted "public options" (for instance Washington's Cascade Care) ended up as privately administered plans with rate caps benchmarked to Medicare, not Medicaid — an instructive gap between the proposal and what passes.

column3: What is "rebalancing," and what tools drive it?
column4:
Shifting LTSS spending from institutional care toward home and community based services. Tools: 1915(c) waivers, 1915(i) and 1915(k) state plan options, Money Follows the Person, MLTSS with contractual HCBS targets, Olmstead litigation and settlements, and presumptive eligibility for HCBS.

HCBS now exceeds institutional spending nationally, but state variation is enormous and the aggregate hides long waiting lists. Rebalancing is the clearest case in Medicaid where the statutory default (institutional care mandatory, HCBS optional) has been overcome almost entirely by workarounds rather than by amending the statute.

column3: What is the "woodwork effect" argument against expanding HCBS?
column4:
The claim that offering home-based services draws in people who would never have entered a nursing home — so HCBS adds new users rather than diverting expensive ones, and total spending rises even though cost per person falls.

The empirical picture is mixed and depends on the time horizon: HCBS expansions do increase the number served, but studies with longer follow-up generally find institutional use and total LTSS spending growth moderating. It is also worth noting the normative asymmetry — "woodwork" describes people with genuine unmet need finally receiving services.

column3: Why is direct care workforce policy a Medicaid design problem?
column4:
Because Medicaid is the dominant purchaser of paid home care, Medicaid rates effectively set direct care wages. Wages near the retail and fast food floor produce turnover exceeding half a year in many markets, which limits HCBS capacity regardless of how generous the benefit is on paper.

Policy responses: wage pass-through requirements, the 2024 Access Rule's 80/20 provision, rate add-ons tied to compensation, training and career ladders, and self-direction (which lets family members be paid). The 80/20 rule is notable as direct regulation of an input price rather than an output price.

column3: Why is there so little private long-term care insurance, and what does Medicaid have to do with it?
column4:
Medicaid pays for LTSS after assets are spent down, so for most households private LTC insurance buys mainly the preservation of assets they would otherwise lose — a large implicit tax on the policy. Adverse selection and pricing failures compound the problem.

This is Brown and Finkelstein's crowd-out result (deck 3). The design implication is that "encourage private LTC insurance" strategies — including the Partnership programs that shield assets equal to insurance benefits paid — face a structural headwind. Washington State's payroll-tax-funded WA Cares is the main U.S. attempt at a public alternative.

column3: Why is dual eligible integration so difficult, and what is the misaligned-incentive problem?
column4:
Medicare and Medicaid pay for different services for the same person under different rules. Neither payer captures the savings its own spending generates: Medicaid pays for home care that prevents hospitalizations Medicare would fund, and Medicare pays for hospital stays that Medicaid's inadequate community services caused.

This is the canonical cost-shifting problem in U.S. health policy. Every integration model — PACE, FIDE SNPs, the Financial Alignment Initiative, integrated appeals and exclusively aligned enrollment — is an attempt to put both revenue streams under one entity so the savings and the spending land in the same place.

column3: What was the Financial Alignment Initiative, and what happened to it?
column4:
A CMS demonstration testing two models for duals: a capitated model with three-way contracts among CMS, the state, and Medicare-Medicaid Plans (MMPs), and a managed fee-for-service model with shared savings. The capitated MMPs sunset at the end of 2025 and states transitioned to integrated D-SNPs.

Evaluations found modest savings and mixed quality results, with performance varying much more across states than across models. The strategic lesson CMS drew was to build integration into the permanent D-SNP framework rather than to keep running a parallel demonstration.

column3: Why is eligibility system architecture a first-order policy variable?
column4:
Because the share of renewals completed ex parte — determined by how well the system connects to payroll, tax, SNAP, and SSA data — largely determines how many eligible people keep coverage in any redetermination event.

The unwinding made this visible: states with comparable eligibility rules but different systems had procedural termination rates differing by a factor of several. Federal 90/10 match for system development and 75/25 for operations is the main lever, and it is one of the highest-leverage uses of federal dollars in the program.

column3: What is the trade-off between state and county administration of Medicaid?
column4:
County administration allows local responsiveness and integration with other local services, but produces within-state variation in processing times, error rates, and outcomes — and complicates the single state agency's accountability.

Several large states (California, New York, North Carolina, Wisconsin, Ohio, Colorado, Minnesota) are county-administered or county-supervised. Within-state variation there is often larger than between-state variation, a useful and underexploited source of identifying variation for research.

column3: What is the standard "iron triangle" framing, and how does it apply to Medicaid design?
column4:
Cost, quality (or access), and coverage: improving two typically worsens the third. Medicaid has historically chosen broad coverage and low cost, paying for it with low provider payment rates — which shows up as access problems.

This makes the trade-offs legible. Raising rates to fix access costs money that must come from coverage or elsewhere. A per capita cap holds cost while nominally holding coverage — so the pressure lands on rates and benefits. Ask of any proposal: which corner is it giving up, and does it say so?

column3: What questions should you ask of any Medicaid reform proposal?
column4:
• Who bears the risk if costs exceed projections?
  • What is the behavioral assumption about enrollees, states, plans, or providers, and is it supported?
  • How does it behave in a recession or an epidemic?
  • What is the administrative burden, and on whom does it fall?
  • Where does the claimed saving actually come from — efficiency, price, or fewer covered person-months?
  • What is the counterfactual: what happens to these people and these costs otherwise?


The fifth question is the most diagnostic. Most large Medicaid savings estimates come from reduced enrollment or reduced provider payment, not from efficiency. That is a legitimate policy choice, but it is a different one from what proposals usually claim.

column3: Distinguish "cost saving" from "cost shifting" in Medicaid proposals.
column4:
A genuine saving reduces total resources consumed. A shift moves who pays: from the federal government to states, from states to providers, from providers to uncompensated care and bad debt, or from the program to enrollees and their families in the form of unpaid caregiving and untreated illness.

Federal Medicaid cuts almost always show up as some combination of state general fund pressure, provider revenue loss, and uninsurance. The uncompensated care channel is quantified — see Garthwaite, Gross, and Notowidigdo, and Finkelstein-Hendren-Luttmer's finding that a large share of Medicaid's value accrues to external parties.

column3: What are the recurring criticisms of governing Medicaid through 1115 waivers?
column4:
• "Demonstrations" often run for decades without generating usable evidence
  • Budget neutrality is an administrative construct with negotiable accounting, so approvals can move real money on contestable arithmetic
  • Policy swings with administrations, since the same authority approves and rescinds work requirements
  • It substitutes executive discretion for legislation on questions of national scope


The defence is genuine: waivers are how expansion alternatives, HCBS, managed care, and delivery reform were all developed, and Congress rarely legislates program design. But note the asymmetry — waivers have proved a much better mechanism for adding coverage and services than for restricting them, since restrictions face the "objectives of the program" test.

column3: What makes a good waiver evaluation design, and why are most weak?
column4:
A good design specifies a credible comparison group (other states, bordering counties, a phased rollout), pre-registers outcomes, and uses administrative rather than solely survey data. Most are weak because the demonstration goes statewide at once with no comparison group, evaluators are hired by the state being evaluated, and results appear years after renewal decisions.

A concrete improvement available to any state: stagger implementation geographically. Phased rollouts are usually administratively necessary anyway, and they convert a program launch into a natural experiment at essentially no cost.

column3: What is the fiscal argument that expansion partly pays for itself at the state level?
column4:
Expansion at 90 percent federal match displaces state spending previously made at lower or zero match — state-funded behavioral health, correctional health care, uncompensated care pools, and state-only programs — and generates provider tax and premium tax revenue on the new volume.

Multiple state-level analyses found net state budget effects near zero or positive in early expansion years. The claim weakens if the enhanced match falls, which is exactly why the 90 percent rate is the pivotal parameter in expansion politics and why trigger laws exist.

column3: What is an expansion "trigger law"?
column4:
A state statute that automatically ends or requires reconsideration of Medicaid expansion if the federal match falls below a specified level (usually 90 percent).

Around a dozen expansion states have one. They function as a commitment device in state politics — expansion is offered as contingent on federal generosity — and they mean a federal match cut would produce faster and larger coverage losses than a state-by-state legislative process would.

column3: What is the design argument for and against benefit "flexibility" for states?
column4:
For: states know their populations and delivery systems; uniform federal benefit rules force spending on low-value services and block substitution toward what a given population needs.
Against: "flexibility" in a binding budget constraint means the power to reduce, and the services most often cut (dental, therapy, personal care, NEMT) are the ones with weak constituencies rather than weak value.

The empirical test worth applying: when states have received flexibility, what did they actually do with it? The historical record is mostly narrowing — which does not settle the argument, but it should inform the prior.

column3: What is the design logic of Medicaid reentry waivers?
column4:
People leaving incarceration face extreme risk in the first weeks out — overdose mortality is many times the general population rate — yet the inmate payment exclusion means coverage typically begins only at release, with no medication supply, no scheduled appointment, and often no active enrollment.

Reentry 1115s let Medicaid pay for a package (case management, medication-assisted treatment, a 30-day medication supply, care coordination) in the 30-90 days pre-release. California's January 2023 approval was the first; many states followed. It is a clean example of the general principle that coverage timing, not just coverage, determines outcomes.

column3: What is the "two Medicaids" observation, and why does it matter for design?
column4:
Medicaid is really two programs sharing a name: acute care coverage for low-income families (large enrollment, low cost per person, resembles insurance) and long-term care financing for people with disabilities and older adults (small enrollment, very high cost, resembles a social service system).

Most reform debate is conducted about the first while most spending growth risk sits in the second. Proposals designed around the acute-care population — work requirements, cost sharing, consumer choice — are largely irrelevant to where the money is, and proposals that would bind the LTSS population are rarely defended explicitly.

column3: If the goal is covering low-income adults, what are the alternatives to Medicaid expansion?
column4:
• Marketplace subsidies extended below 100 percent FPL, with cost-sharing reductions
  • Premium assistance using Medicaid dollars to buy marketplace plans (Arkansas model)
  • A Basic Health Program-style state plan
  • A federal fallback program in non-expansion states (proposed but never enacted)
  • Employer-based approaches with Medicaid wraparound


Each trades off cost per enrollee, provider access, continuity, and administrative complexity. The recurring finding is that alternatives which pay commercial rates buy better access at meaningfully higher cost per person — a real trade, not a free lunch in either direction.

column3: Why do Medicaid savings proposals so often target the financing side rather than benefits or eligibility?
column4:
Because financing changes are less visible. Reducing the provider tax safe harbor or capping directed payments does not appear on any enrollee's notice, produces no immediate identifiable loser, and scores large savings — while the coverage effects arrive later, indirectly, through state budget decisions.

The analytic corollary: to evaluate a financing-side change you have to model the state's fiscal response, which is exactly the step where estimates diverge most. Two credible analysts can differ by an order of magnitude on the same provision depending on whether they assume states backfill.

column3: What does "budget neutrality" hide, and how should you read a waiver's savings claim?
column4:
It compares demonstration spending to a projected without-waiver baseline that the state and CMS negotiate. Generous baseline assumptions create paper savings that can be spent on new demonstration activity, so the entire claim depends on a counterfactual nobody observes.

Practical reading advice: find the baseline growth rate and the treatment of prior-period savings carryover in the special terms and conditions. Those two parameters usually determine whether a demonstration is "budget neutral" far more than anything the demonstration does.

column3: What is the "churn between Medicaid and the marketplace" problem, and what fixes it?
column4:
Income fluctuation across 138 percent FPL moves people between programs with different plans, networks, formularies, and cost sharing — often mid-treatment. Fixes: Basic Health Program, aligned plan participation across both markets, 12-month continuous eligibility, integrated eligibility systems, and auto-enrollment into a marketplace plan on Medicaid termination.

Sommers and Rosenbaum estimated that a large share of low-income adults would experience such a transition within a year. Insurers participating in both markets ("bridge plans") let a person keep the same carrier and network across the line, which addresses the continuity problem without unifying the programs.

column3: What are the main design options for behavioral health in Medicaid?
column4:
• Carve-out to a PIHP or county system — specialized expertise, but fragmented from physical health
  • Carve-in to comprehensive MCOs — integration and one accountable entity, but weaker specialty focus
  • Certified Community Behavioral Health Clinics (CCBHCs) — a prospective, cost-based rate for a required comprehensive service array
  • 1115 SMI/SUD waivers — federal match for short IMD stays in exchange for a continuum-of-care commitment


CCBHCs are the notable recent development: they apply the FQHC financing model (cost-based prospective payment plus a defined mandatory scope) to behavioral health, and were expanded from demonstration to a permanent state option pathway.

column3: Why is quality measurement weaker in Medicaid than in Medicare?
column4:
Enrollment spells are shorter (so annual measures miss people), the population is heterogeneous across children, pregnancy, disability, and LTSS, encounter data from managed care plans have historically been incomplete, and Core Set reporting was voluntary until FY2024.

The consequence is that pay-for-performance in Medicaid often runs on measures that are noisy, weakly related to the outcomes anyone cares about, and not comparable across states. Mandatory Core Set reporting and improved T-MSIS data are the main structural fixes underway.

column3: What special Medicaid rules apply to American Indians and Alaska Natives?
column4:
100 percent FMAP for services received through IHS and tribal facilities, exemption from premiums and cost sharing for those eligible for IHS services, exemption from mandatory managed care enrollment, and required tribal consultation on state plan and waiver changes.

The 100 percent match creates a strong state incentive to route care through IHS and tribal facilities, and CMS has broadened what counts as "received through" an IHS/tribal facility to include care under care coordination agreements — a quiet but substantial policy expansion.

column3: How do other wealthy countries handle the function Medicaid performs?
column4:
Most do not have a separate program for the poor at all: coverage is universal through national insurance or a regulated multi-payer system, and low income affects premiums or cost sharing rather than program membership. Long-term care is typically a separate universal or means-tested social insurance scheme (Germany, Japan, the Netherlands).

Two design lessons. First, a program only for poor people has weaker political protection than a universal one — the standard "programs for the poor are poor programs" argument. Second, several countries fund LTSS through dedicated social insurance rather than means-tested welfare, avoiding the spend-down and asset-test machinery that dominates U.S. LTSS eligibility.

column3: What is the "welfare medicine" critique of Medicaid's structure?
column4:
That means-tested coverage segregated from mainstream insurance produces low payment rates, narrow provider participation, stigma, high administrative burden, and weak political constituencies — outcomes that follow from the structure rather than from any specific policy choice.

The counter-observation is that Medicaid has proven remarkably durable and expandable: it has grown to cover a quarter of the country, survived repeated block grant attempts, and outperforms private coverage on cost per enrollee and on financial protection. Both accounts are partly right, which is why the reform literature keeps returning to whether Medicaid should be improved or absorbed.

column3: Does Medicaid control costs well relative to other payers?
column4:
On level, clearly yes — cost per enrollee is well below private insurance for comparable people, driven almost entirely by lower prices. On growth rate, Medicaid's per-enrollee growth has generally tracked or run slightly below private insurance and Medicare.

Important framing point: aggregate Medicaid spending growth is dominated by enrollment growth, not per-enrollee cost growth. Confusing the two is the most common error in cost-control debates, and it matters because per capita caps target the component that is already comparatively well controlled.

column3: Why is Medicaid structurally bad at investing in prevention?
column4:
Enrollees churn, so the payer that funds prevention often is not the one that reaps the savings; savings that do accrue may land on Medicare (for people who age in) or on employers; and state budgets are annual, so a multi-year payoff has no place to land.

This "wrong pockets" problem justifies federal rather than state financing of preventive investment, longer continuous eligibility so a payer holds the person long enough to benefit, and dual integration so Medicare savings can be captured. It is also the strongest structural argument for the HRSN and social-needs agenda being financed federally.

column3: What is the difference between "coverage" and "access," and why does the distinction discipline policy design?
column4:
Coverage is a legal and financial status; access is whether care is actually obtained. Medicaid can deliver near-complete coverage while delivering poor access if payment rates are too low, networks are inadequate, transportation fails, or prior authorization is burdensome.

This is why coverage-only metrics mislead in both directions. It also explains why the honest version of the "Medicaid doesn't improve health" argument is really a claim about access and effective care, not about insurance — and why the policy response would be higher rates and better delivery, not less coverage.
